newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnia's Plavsic seeks support against hardliners.
newsitem.headline: Bosnia's Plavsic seeks support against hardliners.

text.p: Bosnian Serb president Biljana Plavsic moved to rally support in her battle with government hardliners allied with indicted war criminal Radovan Karadzic.

Plavsic won some sympathy from Western governments and secured cautious backing from the Bosnian Serb army after meeting the general staff on Wednesday in her offices in the northern town of Banja Luka.

British peacekeeping troops patrolled the town in armoured vehicles and NATO helicopters buzzed overhead to discourage possible violence between Plavsic's supporters and Karadzic's hardliners, who control a heavily-armed police force.

The army general staff issued a carefully-worded statement saying it would respect the authority of the president as the supreme commander in Bosnian Serb territory and called for a political resolution of the crisis.
The army carries important symbolism but Karadzic and his allies control a large police force which has become more powerful than the military in peacetime.
Recently purged by Karadzic, the army lacks financial support and its movements are severely restricted by the NATO-led peacekeeping force.
Opposition parties in Banja Luka called the power struggle dangerous, urged new elections and said they wanted to meet Plavsic on Thursday to discuss the tense stand-off.
France sided with Plavsic in the power struggle, saying she had shown a willingness to cooperate with efforts to carry out the Dayton peace treaty in Bosnia-Herzegovina.
The U.S. diplomat organising municipal elections in September, Robert Frowick, also said Plavsic deserved support.

He said Plavsic was "doing her best to implement the Dayton agreement in the face of resistance by elements of the ruling Serb Democratic Party, some of whom opposed the agreement from its inception".
Karadzic's party nominated Plavsic for the presidency last year in the belief she would prove an obedient successor, but she has condemned the leadership as corrupt war profiteers.
"When I was elected, many thought I would be simply a puppet in the hands of the former president, but that isn't the kind of person I am," Plavsic told reporters on Wednesday.
Plavsic, herself an ultra-nationalist ideologue, has argued for cooperating with the international community to preserve Serb interests under the U.S.-brokered peace treaty.
The ruling party's central committee has demanded Plavsic drop her calls for the suspension of the interior minister, a Karadzic loyalist, or step down from office.
Vowing to fight to the end, Plavsic kept up fierce criticism of her opponents in hopes of capitalising on dissatisfaction among an impoverished population.

Karadzic and his main ally, Momcilo Krajisnik, the Serb member of Bosnia's collective presidency, were preparing a parliamentary session for Friday in which Plavsic would be castigated by the ruling party.

The parliament was expected to launch proceedings for a recall vote against Plavsic. Under the Bosnian Serb republic's constitution, the president can only be removed by a popular vote, diplomats said.
Karadzic, who led separatist Serbs during the 1992-95 war, was forced to step down from office under international pressure last year and promised to stay out of politics.
Scoffing at his indictment by the U.N. war crimes tribunal, Karadzic continues to wield covert influence over his party in a bid to obstruct the peace accords.
